reader.summary: The defining story of the week in the Netherlands was personal and political: Prime Minister Rob Jetten, the country's first openly LGBTQ head of government, announced that he and his partner are expecting their first child, to be born in 2027, via a surrogate mother. The news was picked up by Reuters, the BBC, Bloomberg and French broadcaster TV5Monde, and it framed Jetten as a symbol of progressive Dutch society at a moment when European politics is shifting. Beyond the family news, the major Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police, raising questions about the resilience of one of the country's largest listed companies. The Eredivisie football season continued with a full round of match previews covering fixtures involving PSV, Feyenoord, Ajax, Sparta Rotterdam, Twente, Utrecht and several other clubs. A Bloomberg column urged readers to look past Amsterdam's party reputation and take its food culture seriously. A Financial Times piece on INVE Technologies described a $20 million modified Dutch auction tender offer, though the reference to a 'Dutch auction' is a financial mechanism rather than a story about the Netherlands itself. Overall it was a calm week with one high-visibility personal-political announcement and a moderate corporate security incident.

display.eli5:
Right now in the Netherlands, two big stories are in the headlines. The prime minister just announced he is going to be a dad for the first time, and a huge supermarket company called Ahold Delhaize told the police that hackers got into their computer systems. The rest of the news is mostly about football matches.

The baby news is a one-time thing, so after a few days of everyone talking about it, it will start to fade. The hacker story is different because companies usually have to explain more details over the following days, and the stock price can move a lot.

Next week you will probably see the supermarket company put out a longer statement about what exactly got hacked and whether customers' data is safe. The prime minister's baby story will still get some mentions but will stop being the top story. And the football league will have another round of games, which always gets covered.

A surprise would be if a politician in parliament asks the government why it does not check more closely on whether big companies are protecting their computer systems. That is not impossible, but it is not the most likely thing to happen.
